extracted.intended_audience: humor theorists, comedy writers, and anyone evaluating or designing jokes with attention to moral content (philosophers of humor, critics, joke designers)
extracted.subtask_description: A framework for evaluating how a joke's moral features affect its funniness and for designing jokes to maximize amusement while avoiding genuine moral wrongs. Emphasizes distinguishing structural comic mechanisms, taboo-transgression thrill, and genuine moral status of targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral flaws decrease (never enhance) amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral flaws in the joke (cruelty, dishonesty, malice toward undeserving targets) never increase funniness and can decrease it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smuts's central symmetric claim: once you control for transgression-thrill and audience sensibilities, genuine moral flaws subtract from amusement. Example: a racist joke is less funny (for morally sensitive audiences) than the same structure targeting 'stuck-up CEOs.' Treat morally flawed content as something the joke is funny despite, not because of.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral virtues can enhance (never decrease) amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral virtues displayed by the joke (justice, kindness in target selection, fair treatment, moral courage in satire) can increase funniness and never decrease it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical targeting that exhibits moral virtue (e.g., punching up at corrupt politicians) enhances amusement. Example: a satirical takedown of a corrupt politician is funnier than attacking a private citizen for the same behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish genuine moral flaws from apparent/benign violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all seemingly transgressive or dark jokes are genuinely morally flawed; some violate convention without creating a real victim or harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for a real victim, undeserved harm, or lack of protected 'play' frame. Many 'dark' jokes are morally innocent because targets are hypothetical, powerful/deserving, or the audience adopts a protected playful stance; those are not genuine moral flaws and need not reduce funniness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transgression-thrill confound — separate taboo-breaking from moral wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: Taboo-breaking (the thrill of forbiddenness) is conceptually and causally distinct from moral-flaw status and can add edginess without being morally wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating funniness, control for taboo-breaking effects: determine whether the 'edge' of a joke is coming from harmless convention-breaking or from genuine moral wrong. The thrill of transgression can make a joke feel edgier even when it is morally innocent; do not conflate this with a 'naughtiness bonus' for moral wrongs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural funniness (comic mechanism) should be evaluated separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the comic mechanism (incongruity, resolution, surprise, timing) as an independent dimension from moral status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A joke's structural resources produce funniness; moral-flaw status may detract from or be tolerated by audiences, but structure is what makes the joke funny in itself. When diagnosing or designing jokes, identify the structural source of amusement and then evaluate how moral factors modulate the response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate target selection for maximal amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose targets whose denigration is morally appropriate (powerful, deserving, hypothetical, or the self) and avoid genuine victims of unjust suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design guidance: redirect the comic structure toward targets that are deserving or powerful to increase funniness for typical audiences. Avoid attacking real victims or those suffering unjustly, since that moral flaw will typically subtract from amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify tone: satire (moral virtue) vs aggression (moral flaw)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the joke functions as satire (punching up with moral purpose) or aggression (gratuitous harm or mockery of vulnerable victims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire often enhances amusement because it aligns with moral virtues (exposing wrongdoing), whereas aggression toward undeserving targets tends to decrease funniness. Use this classification when predicting audience responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience moral sensibility as a moderating criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience's moral sensibility (degree of sensitivity, background norms) modulates whether a moral flaw reduces amusement and how much transgression-thrill is tolerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing humor, consider audience differences and control for them in comparisons. Smuts emphasizes responses 'for audiences with intact moral sensibilities' — different audiences may exhibit different tolerances, so evaluation must account for this variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfactual/redirection test for diagnosing moral effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether the same comic structure redirected at a more deserving or non-victim target would be funnier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an experimental diagnostic: compare the joke as-is to variants that change the target while keeping structure and transgression level constant. If the redirected version is funnier, the original likely suffered from a genuine moral flaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic checklist of moral-status questions
rubrics_metrics.description: A short set of questions to determine the moral contribution to a joke's funniness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions (from Smuts): Does the joke have a real victim of unjust suffering as its target? If so, is the joke funnier or less funny for it (controlling for transgression-thrill)? Could the same comic structure be redirected to a more deserving target and be funnier? Is the joke satire (moral virtue) or aggression (moral flaw)? Does the audience's moral sensibility increase or decrease the response to this joke?
